name: Bond price
seoDesc: Bond price: work out bond price from the annual coupon rate and the coupon per period. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: bond price is what the Bond price calculator works out, and it gets there from the annual coupon rate, the coupon per period, the years to maturity and the yield to maturity. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Bond price calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bond price calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports bond price in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the annual coupon rate, the coupon per period, the years to maturity and the yield to maturity (YTM).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bond price calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Bond price=(face value, years to maturity, yield to maturity (YTM), annual coupon rate, coupon frequency)
Coupon frequency=annual coupon rate × face value ÷ coupon per period
Annual Coupon=annual coupon rate × face value

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Face value = 10, Annual coupon rate = 10 %, Coupon frequency set to Annually and Coupon per period = 10. The calculator returns Annual Coupon = 1.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Annual Coupon = 1 should be roughly the size you expected from Face value = 10 and Annual coupon rate = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bond price calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the annual coupon rate, the coupon per period and the years to maturity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bond price calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns bond price, derived from the annual coupon rate, the coupon per period and the years to maturity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bond price calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the annual coupon rate, the coupon per period, the years to maturity and the yield to maturity, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter face value in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Face value opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Annual Coupon = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bond price calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
